data.title: JPMorgan: MSG Rangers Is a Trophy Asset at a Deep Discount
data.description: According to CNBC, JPMorgan initiated coverage of MSG Rangers with an overweight rating and set a $310 price target, implying 25% upside from Thursday’s close. Analyst David Karnovsky said shares traded at an approximately 30% discount to private-market value estimates, which he said may be understated. He cited limited team supply, growing ownership capital, media-rights trends and venue economics as factors supporting professional team valuations. Karnovsky also said a potential minority stake sale could provide a higher reference price for the team and fund operations and capital returns. Other potential catalysts he cited included NHL U.S. media-rights negotiations, team expansion and improved on-ice performance. MSG Rangers and MSG Knickerbockers became separate publicly traded firms in October. The stock is up 14% month to date, and all five analysts covering it have a buy or strong buy rating, according to LSEG data.

data.title: Dan Akerson: Finding Mary Barra's Successor at GM Will Be Tough
data.description: According to CNBC, former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson said replacing CEO Mary Barra will be difficult, citing her record and challenges facing the auto industry, including artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, China's rise and autonomous vehicles. He said a successor should be dynamic and that hiring from outside could be risky if internal candidates have similar leadership and technical expertise. A Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday said General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify potential outside candidates alongside internal prospects. The company declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

data.title: Michael Lewis, Author of 'The Big Short': Crypto Reflects Distrust of Fiat Currency
data.description:
Solana said on X that Michael Lewis, author of “The Big Short,” made the remarks at Breakpoint 2026.

According to Odaily, Lewis said the financial crisis was resolved because an experienced person stepped in to stabilize the situation, and asked what would happen if the government itself became the problem. He added that cryptocurrency partly reflects people’s distrust of fiat currency.

data.title: Binance Outlines Security Measures Following Recent Attack
data.description:
Binance announced on X that it has taken additional containment and hardening measures following the recent attack. Its ongoing review includes further segmentation, access control and monitoring improvements across internal environments.

Binance said it is focused on strengthening environment isolation, tightening privileged access pathways, enhancing verification controls and reducing the risk of similar attack vectors. For security reasons, it will not share detailed architecture or control design specifics publicly.

data.title: STOCKS | Oracle Hits 52-Week Low, Down 46.8% Over the Past Year
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, Oracle shares fell intraday to $107.86 on November 20, setting a 52-week low. The stock was down 11.8% over the past week and 46.8% over the past year.

After sustained selling, Oracle's price-to-earnings ratio fell to 17.4 and its price/earnings-to-growth ratio to 0.39. The company recently completed a $10 billion share offering, which drew demand far exceeding its size. The top 10 investors received 65% of the shares, while the top 20 received 85%.

Stephens raised its rating on Oracle from Equal-Weight to Overweight and lifted its price target to $213, citing growth potential in its cloud infrastructure business. Bernstein maintained an Outperform rating and a $325 price target, while KeyBanc maintained an Overweight rating and a $300 target.

Susquehanna warned that regulatory changes after the U.S. midterm elections could threaten AI infrastructure construction. AI data center projects involving about 12 gigawatts of computing capacity face cancellation risk.

data.title: Acadian Asset Management: 'Smart Money' Is Selling as U.S. Stock Issuance Rises
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management, wrote in a letter to investors this month that U.S. companies have shifted from stock buybacks in 2024 to issuing shares, prompting him to ask why “smart money” is selling.

An Acadian analysis found that net new stock issuance equaled 3.1% of total stock market capitalization as of last weekend. The figure remains below peaks during the dot-com bubble and the COVID-19-era bubble, but the analysis says the buyback era has ended and an issuance era is beginning. Anthropic’s large IPO added to the supply of shares this week. Its offering was initially priced at $83 per share, above the prior expected range, and raised $81 billion amid strong investor demand. The stock began falling Friday, weighing on the broader equity market.

Stock buybacks had reduced the number of shares available to trade and could boost earnings per share by shrinking the share-count denominator. A 2000 paper by Malcolm Baker and Jeffrey Wurgler found that markets tended to deliver lower returns when companies issued more equity relative to debt. The Baker-Wurgler Equity Share measure peaked at about 18% in 2021; Lamont said it has recently risen but remains below that level.

Federal Reserve data show a similar pattern in the year-over-year change in total stock and bond issuance: debt issuance rose first in 2020, followed by stock issuance in 2021. More recently, debt issuance began recovering in 2024, followed by a sharp increase in stock issuance in 2026.

Recent deals include Oracle’s application to sell $20 billion in shares through an at-the-market program and its separate $10 billion common-stock offering in November; Meta’s October pricing of a $25 billion common-stock offering and $12.5 billion mandatory convertible preferred-stock offering; Alphabet’s announcement in June that it would raise $84.8 billion in equity; and SpaceX’s June IPO, which raised $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment option. Lamont wrote that companies had been net repurchasers of shares before 2026 but have now become net issuers. He said he could not rule out the possibility that the market is in an AI bubble.

data.title: Cynthia Lummis Says Democrats Sought Crypto Certification Office but Opposed CLARITY Act
data.description: U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis appeared to express dissatisfaction with Democrats in a post. According to Odaily, she said Democrats had previously asked the SEC to establish an office overseeing certifications related to crypto assets to prevent gaps in regulatory work. The CLARITY Act established the office, but Democratic lawmakers ultimately voted against the bill.

data.title: Anthropic and OpenAI IPO Race Puts Investment Banks in an Awkward Position
data.description: Anthropic executives began seriously planning an IPO in summer 2025 after realizing that venture capital and investors such as Amazon could not fund enough chips to run and train its models. According to Odaily, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are handling IPO projects for both companies, putting the banks in an awkward position. Banks generally separate teams working on competing IPOs, but some bankers have sought information about rival projects from fund managers who had heard presentations. Anthropic executives privately believed that summer that OpenAI was unlikely to go public first. OpenAI had recently shifted its focus to selling models to enterprise customers, a change that was likely to delay its IPO.

data.title: Wintermute Policy Chief Calls for Crypto Lobbying Shake-Up in Washington
data.description:
According to ChainCatcher, Wintermute Policy and Advocacy Lead Ron Hammond said at Thursday’s Capital Crypto Forum that the crypto industry needs to “clean house” in Washington after a series of lobbying setbacks. He said divisions within the industry suggest it is either not united enough or unable to prevail against more powerful interests.

The remarks came about a month after the SEC introduced a five-year innovation exemption in September that opened a path for trading tokenized U.S. stocks. The policy faced opposition from traditional financial firms and lawmakers, with JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, McDonald’s and dozens of other companies objecting to third parties tokenizing their shares. Hammond said the final exemption was narrow and restrictive, offered little help to firms such as Wintermute, but was a good first step.

Hammond also criticized the industry’s choice of political allies, saying some lawmakers who campaigned on supporting crypto later opposed tokenization. Earlier this week, four Democratic senators warned SEC Chair Paul Atkins that the exemption had gaps in customer identification and anti-money-laundering requirements. Kristin Johnson, nominated by U.S. President Donald Trump to be an SEC commissioner, said at a Senate Banking Committee hearing that she welcomed formal rulemaking that includes public comment. Hammond added that U.K. officials are using gaps in U.S. regulation to attract digital-asset companies back to Britain.

data.title: AI | Novartis CEO: AI Could Shorten Drug Development From 12 Years to Eight
data.description:
Novartis CEO Vasant Narasimhan said artificial intelligence could reduce drug-development time from 12 years to eight and improve the odds of bringing new medicines to market. He told Bloomberg’s Francine Lacqua on “The Pulse” that AI is already helping Novartis speed clinical trials, analyze data and identify drug candidates, according to Bloomberg.

Narasimhan, who also sits on Anthropic’s board, discussed Novartis’ growth outlook, drug pricing in Europe and the US, and AI regulation.

data.title: Bank of America Analysts: 2027 Risk-Asset Performance Hinges on Two Questions
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, Bank of America Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett and his team said on November 20 that risk-asset performance in 2027 would depend on when the rate-hiking cycle ends and whether the Federal Reserve can stop raising rates before the economy enters a recession. Bank of America expects global central banks to make a cumulative 71 rate hikes from June 2026 through May 2027. It said risk assets face sustained pressure as previously optimistic market sentiment meets tighter global monetary policy.

Bank of America said that if the Fed continues to treat the stock market as “too big to fail,” pressure from credit and equity markets could prompt it to end rate hikes early if investment-grade credit default swap index (CDX) spreads rise above 80 basis points and the S&P 500 falls below 6,845. But if the Fed prioritizes curbing inflation, markets may not begin pricing in an end to rate hikes until its March 18 or April 28, 2027, meetings, raising the risk of a U.S. hard landing.

Hartnett said current market conditions resemble the period after the technology bubble burst in 2000, when tech stocks peaked and fell while the Fed continued raising rates, before the U.S. entered a recession in 2001. Bank of America said markets underestimate the probability of a hard landing and that consensus forecasts for 5% to 6% U.S. nominal GDP growth and more than 15% corporate earnings growth in 2027 are too optimistic. It identified initial jobless claims above 250,000 and investment-grade credit spreads widening beyond 100 basis points as warning signs of a damaging feedback loop between the economy and financial markets.

The net share of global equity indexes in oversold territory is 68%, nearing the 88% threshold for a Bank of America market-breadth buy signal. Hartnett expects the signal in the coming days and a possible stock-market rebound after Thanksgiving. A larger rally, the bank said, requires the 10-year Treasury yield to fall below 4.5%, WTI crude to drop below $70 a barrel, and the dollar to peak and decline.

Bank of America’s bull-and-bear indicator has fallen from 7.4 to 7.1, while fund managers’ cash holdings remain at 3.6%. Equity funds attracted a record $310 billion over the past four weeks. The bank said investors may need to reduce holdings further before the market bottoms. It also expects 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds to post a negative return for a sixth straight year, the longest such losing streak since 1963–1969.
